title: The mobile visit for a nonprofit
metaTitle: The mobile visit to a nonprofit site
excerpt: The first phone screen has to show the work and a way to give, join, or read the program. A tall desktop hero will hide that decision below the fold.
alt: Smooth overlapping waves of blue, violet, and warm orange, for a piece on keeping a small screen calm and readable.
caption: Broad bands of color, simple enough to read small. A phone page should be this uncluttered. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on a nonprofit's first phone screen?
faqs.answer: The program in one sentence, a concrete scene or fact, and the primary action. Give, join, and read can all exist. One of them should lead. Three equal buttons will push the scene off the screen and stall the decision.

faqs.question: Where do hours and address go on a phone?
faqs.answer: At the top of the program page, as text. A map can supplement the address, and it should not be the only copy. People open these pages while standing outside or while talking to a relative. The facts have to be available before the story.

faqs.question: How short should a mobile gift or application be?
faqs.answer: Short enough to finish in one hand. Name, contact, the program or the amount, and one question you truly need. Show the amount and the cadence before someone commits. A monthly gift has to look monthly on a narrow screen.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A nonprofit mobile website is where many donors and many participants will decide whether the work is real. The first screen on a phone still has to show the work in the world and a way to give, join, or read the program. A desktop composition that opens with a tall photograph, a gala line, and a donate button underneath will spend that decision on the wrong things. Design the narrow screen as the real page.

People will open your link on a bus, in a school office, or in a hallway outside your own event. They will forward a single program to a relative. If that view cannot answer what you do and how to enter, the wide homepage is a poster. Posters do not take applications.

## The first screen at a narrow width

Set a phone width and read the homepage without scrolling. You should see the program in a sentence, a scene or a fact that makes it concrete, and the primary action. If the action sits under a full-viewport image, shorten the image. If the sentence is a slogan that wraps into four lines, rewrite the sentence. The wide layout can have more air later. It should not have different news.

The scene has to survive the crop. Use the vertical frame where the work sits in the center. A wide shot of a room with the relevant action at the edge will become a picture of ceiling. The visitor's first impression of whether you are real is partly this crop. Treat it as content, not as a responsive side effect.

Say whether the person is in the right place for help or for a gift, without making either of them hunt. A short line, "Free weeknight clinic, enroll below," plus a secondary text link to give, can be enough. Equal shouting from three buttons will push the scene off the screen. Choose a primary for the season. Keep the others one tap away in the header or directly under the primary.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is unforgiving about this opening. People often leave in 10–20 seconds. A page earns a longer look by stating its value immediately. On a phone, value is the work and the door. A manifesto and a modal will spend the window before the clinic's hours appear.

## Give, join, or read without a scavenger hunt

The primary control should be visible without opening a menu, and it should stay reachable as the person scrolls. Apply, give, or read, in the verb your season requires. A thumb should be able to hit it. A control crushed against the logo, or hidden behind a chat bubble, will be mis-tapped or ignored.

The destination has to finish the job on the same phone. An application that assumes a desktop, a donation form that spills off the side, or a program description that is only a multi-column PDF will strand the person you just convinced. Build an HTML version of the practical facts. Place, time, who it is for, what it costs, what to bring. Offer the PDF as a supplement for people who need the packet, and make the packet readable, with a size a phone connection can bear.

Reading the program is a legitimate path. Do not treat it as a consolation prize buried in the footer. A donor who is undecided and a participant who is cautious both need a page that stands alone. On a phone, that page should front-load the facts and keep the narrative after. They can keep reading if the facts matched. They cannot scroll backward through a story to discover that the program is full.

Confirmation screens are part of the mobile visit. After someone gives or applies, the next view should say what happened and what happens next, in the same verbs, at a readable size. A blank thank-you, or a desktop receipt smashed into a narrow column, makes people submit twice or assume they failed. Say the amount or the application window. Offer one sensible next link, not a maze of share buttons.

## Program pages on a small screen

Hours, address, cost, and boundary belong at the top of a program page. These are the facts a person came to check, often while standing outside the building or while talking to a family member. A long story above the address is a barrier. Put the story after the facts, or beside them in the way a narrow screen allows, which usually means after.

Maps should be supplements. The address in text, the transit note in text, the entrance note in text. A map image that is the only copy of the address fails when it does not load, and it fails for anyone using a screen reader. The [W3C's overview of WCAG](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treats perceivable, understandable content as a baseline. On this page the baseline is practical. A person can find the door and understand the offer without guessing.

Status belongs at the top too. Open, full, returning in March, walk-in or appointment. Update it. A phone visitor is more likely to act today than a person browsing on a sofa next month. Stale status is a broken promise delivered at the moment of need. Make the status a field someone can change without a developer, and name the person who changes it.

Tables of fees and gift levels should stack. A wide grid of suggested amounts will overflow or shrink. One level per block, with what it supports, and a way to enter another amount. The shape of the price has to be legible in one hand. If it is not, the pricing page is still a desktop document, whatever the analytics say about mobile traffic.

## Images, speed, and interruptions

The photograph of the work is likely the largest element. web.dev's [Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) separate loading, responsiveness, and stability. Largest Contentful Paint asks when that main scene appears. Interaction to Next Paint asks whether the Give or Apply tap responds. Cumulative Layout Shift asks whether the button jumps while images and banners settle. A late hero, a moving button, and a heavy gala video are ways to lose the visitor before the program sentence lands.

Reserve the image space. Use the smaller crop on the small screen. Skip the autoplay film. Skip the third-party widgets that cover the action. If you use a banner for consent, keep it short and do not let it permanently shove the program below the fold. People who prefer reduced motion should get the scene and the action at once. The work is the point. The fade is optional.

Test on a phone that is not new, on a connection that is ordinary. Office wifi will flatter a heavy page. A participant on a prepaid plan will not share your office wifi. Look at the homepage, one program, the give flow, and a proof. If you feel impatient, they will leave. Fix the file or cut the block. Do not add a loading animation to apologize for the weight.

Popups that ask for an email address before the work is visible are especially hostile on a phone, where they are harder to dismiss. Remove them. If you want a mailing list, ask after a person has read the program or completed a gift, and accept no. The mobile visit is often a single task. Do not steal it for a side task.

## Forms that can be finished in one hand

Applications and gifts should ask for the minimum. Name, contact, the program or the amount, and one practical question you truly need. Every extra required field is a chance to abandon, and abandonment on a phone is final more often than on a desktop, because the person was already between other tasks.

Show labels that persist. Use the right keyboard for email and phone and numbers. Allow a person to fix an error without retyping the whole form. Say the error next to the field. These are ordinary interface standards, and they are also how you keep a stressful form from becoming a trap. If a document upload is required, say so early, and offer an alternative when a phone cannot produce the file. "Bring it to intake" or "we will email you a link" can be the humane version. Write that alternative on the page.

Payment should show the amount, the cadence, and the designation before the person commits. A monthly gift must look monthly. A fee must look like a fee, not like a donation. The confirmation should match. Test with a small real transaction and a test application. Do it on the phone you keep in your pocket, not only in a desktop emulator in the office.

## Review the phone before you celebrate the wide layout

Run a script in your hand. From the homepage, say what the program is. Start the primary action and reach a confirmation, or reach the practical facts if the action is "read." Find the address. Find this year's report. Open a program link directly, as if it were texted to you, and repeat. Note every moment you turn the phone sideways or pinch to read.

Do this with the person who answers the phone. They know which fact is missing, because they repeat it all day. Hours, entrance, what to bring, whether it costs anything. If the mobile page omits a fact the desk says aloud, the page is incomplete. Add the fact at the top. Do not schedule it for a later phase.

Hanabi designs and builds the narrow screen as part of the site, not as a shrink of the desktop. You should leave with words you can edit, a fast first view, and files in a portal so the next status change is not a scavenger hunt. The craft is the same one the studio uses on a company site. Clarity, speed, and a page that respects reduced motion.

Look at [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) for the standard of a public page that stays specific on a small screen. Then open your own homepage beside it on a phone. The comparison will be obvious within a few seconds. That is the right length of time, because it is the length of time you have.

When the small screen can carry the work, the next failure is the handoff. [A contact path for a nonprofit](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-nonprofit) is the next piece, because a short, honest account of what happens after someone writes is how a convinced visitor becomes a participant, a volunteer, or a donor.
